$note: How a release is decided here: release-please reads the conventional commits since a component's
last tag, opens a pull request that bumps that component's version and writes its RELEASES.md,
and cutting the tag is what MERGING that pull request does. `release.yml` already in this
repository is what the tag then starts.
THE NARRATIVE CHANGELOG IS NOT TOUCHED. `src_vs_code/CHANGELOG.md` is 127 entries of
hand-written prose and it stays the human record: `changelog-path` sends every generated file to
RELEASES.md instead. This is option A of
reason it is not negotiable here is measured: release.yml extracts the release notes with
`text.indexOf('## [' + v + ']')` and FALLS BACK TO A LINK rather than failing. A release-please
heading is `## [1.9.7](…compare…) (date)`, and that probe matches it at index 0 — a markdown link
is [text](url), so the probe is a prefix. Point release-please at CHANGELOG.md and it would
overwrite the prose while the extraction kept working and the build stayed green.
$decided: SEPARATE PULL REQUESTS, one per component, and it is not a preference. These four ship at
genuinely different cadences — extension 1.9.7 against cli 0.1.6 — so a combined pull request
would tie a cli patch to an extension release nobody asked for. It also keeps the tags coming one
at a time: GitHub creates NO events at all when more than three tags arrive in a single git push,
and four components is exactly the count that would test that rule.
RELEASE TYPES ARE NOT UNIFORM, because the components are not. The extension's package.json IS
its version and release.yml REFUSES a tag that disagrees with it, so `node` fits it exactly and
the guard then passes by construction. Server, cli and mcp carry no version anywhere in the tree
— the build injects it from the tag (-p:Version="${GITHUB_REF_NAME#server-v}") — so `simple`
with a version.txt is what gives them one. That file is a RECORD, not a new input: the build
still takes the version from the tag, and release-please keeps the two in step.
The sidecar's Cargo.toml drifted for two releases (0.1.0 in the file, v0.1.2 on the tag) and
nobody noticed because nothing read the file. That is an argument against an UNMANAGED duplicate,
not against a managed one — and the blindness it describes is the state these three are in today.
include-component-in-tag is TRUE here, unlike the sidecar. Four products share one tag namespace,
so `server-v0.7.1` and `cli-v0.1.7` have to be distinguishable; the sidecar ships one product and
its release workflow triggers on a bare `v*`.
$draft: DRAFT, and this is the correction that cost two empty releases to learn. release-please CREATES
the GitHub release when it cuts the tag — that is HOW it cuts it. `release.yml` here is built on
the opposite guarantee, added deliberately and for a measured reason: the release must not exist
until EVERY asset is ready, because when each matrix leg published its own asset,
server-v0.5.0 shipped 4 of them, v0.5.1 shipped 5 and v0.5.2 shipped 5 — every server release
this repository ever made was missing osx-x64, and each one read as a success.
The two collided on 2026-09-21: `gh release create` failed with `a release with the same tag
name already exists`, and server-v0.8.0 and cli-v0.2.0 sat PUBLISHED WITH ZERO ASSETS — exactly
the state that guarantee exists to prevent.
With `draft: true` the order works for both: release-please cuts the tag and leaves a DRAFT
nobody can download, `release.yml` uploads the assets, its existing count assertion runs against
the real release, and only then does it flip the draft off. Nothing is public until it is whole.
The sidecar never showed this because it publishes with `softprops/action-gh-release`, which
UPDATES an existing release instead of refusing. It worked there by luck, not by design.
$force-tag-creation: WITHOUT THIS, `draft: true` DEADLOCKS THE WHOLE CHAIN, and the action's own schema says why:
"GitHub does not create a Git tag for draft releases until they are published. This 'lazy tag
creation' causes release-please to fail to find the previous release… Setting this to `true`
ensures the tag is created immediately."
So: no tag, and `release.yml` triggers on `push: tags`. It would never run, the draft would
never get its assets, and nothing would ever publish it — a fix worse than the defect it
replaced, and silent in the same way. Caught in review before it shipped, verified against the
schema rather than taken on trust.
$exclude: A COMMIT THAT TOUCHES NOTHING BUT CI IS NOT A RELEASE. `feat(ci): …` on a workflow edit proposes
a MINOR release of a product whose code did not move — that happened three times across this
family on 2026-09-21, twice after the rule had been written down. A note that fails three times
is not a rule, so this is configuration.
EXACTLY ONE ENTRY, AND EXACTLY WHAT IT COVERS — measured against release-please's own
`CommitExclude` (src/util/commit-exclude.ts), transcribed and run, not read and hoped:
a commit touching only `.github/**`            -> SKIPPED
a commit touching `.github/**` AND src_cli/**  -> released
The first list here had four entries. Three of them were DEAD: `isRelevant` tests
`file.indexOf(path + '/') === 0`, so an exclude path is a DIRECTORY PREFIX and a file path can
never match itself. `release-please-config.json` excluded nothing at all; neither did any
`version.txt`. They are gone rather than left in looking like protection.
SO THE SETUP-COMMIT SHAPE IS NOT COVERED, and saying otherwise was the error: the commit that
installed release-please here touched `.github` AND a version.txt inside each component, so every
relevant file was NOT excluded and all three lines proposed a release. Against that shape the
commit TYPE is still the only defence. What this does cover is the recurring case — an ordinary
workflow edit — which is the one that will keep happening.
AND `Release-As:` IS NOT AN ESCAPE HATCH from it, which this note used to claim.
`excludeCommits()` filters the commit list BEFORE any release strategy sees it, so a dropped
commit's footers are never parsed. (CodeRabbit raised it; the source confirms it.) If a CI-only
change genuinely has to ship, put something outside `.github` in the same commit, or release it
alongside the next real change.
THE TRADE, said out loud: a change to `.github` that genuinely alters a product — a compiler
flag, a build argument — is skipped. That is the smaller of the two errors; the other inflates a
version every time anybody edits a workflow.
